translations.text: We read in the book called the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles ordained seven deacons in the congregation of those from the Jewish people who turned to faith in Christ after his passion, his resurrection from death, and his ascension to heaven.
The first of these deacons was Stephen, whom we honour on this day. He was very faithful and filled with the Holy Spirit.
The other six were called by these names: Stephen was the first, the second Philip, the third Prochorus, the fourth Nicanor, the fifth Timon [Timotheus], the sixth Parmenas, the seventh Nicolas.
These seven they chose and set before the apostles, and they were then ordained as deacons with prayers and blessings.
Then the preaching of God grew daily, and the number of Christian people in Jerusalem was greatly multiplied.
Then the blessed Stephen was filled with God's grace and with great strength, and he worked wonders and great signs among the people.
Then some of the unbelieving Jews rose up and tried to overcome the blessed martyr's teaching with their heresy; but they could not withstand his wisdom, nor the Holy Spirit who spoke through him.
Then they put forward false witnesses, who lied about him and said that he spoke blasphemous words about Moses and about God.
Then the people were greatly stirred up, along with the chief men and the Jewish scribes, and they seized Stephen and dragged him to their council; and the false witnesses testified against him:
"This man does not cease to speak blasphemous words against this holy place and God's law. We heard him say that Christ will destroy this place and overturn the ordinances that Moses taught us."
Then those who sat in the council looked at him, and saw his face like the face of an angel. Then the high priest said to the blessed martyr,
"Is it as they say?" Then the holy man Stephen wished to set right their unbelieving hearts by the example and remembrance of their forefathers, and to turn them with all love to the way of truth.
He then began to tell them about the patriarch Abraham: how the heavenly God chose him as his companion, and promised him that all nations would be blessed in his offspring because of his obedience.
Likewise he renewed before them the memory of the other patriarchs, in a lengthy account;
and how Moses, through God's might, wondrously led their forefathers across the Red Sea, and how they afterwards were forty years in the wilderness, fed daily with heavenly food;
and how God led them to the land of the Jews, and utterly wiped out the heathen nations before their eyes;
and about the glory of David, the great king, and the splendour of Solomon, who raised that great temple to God. Then at last he said,
"You resist the Holy Spirit with stiff necks and unbelieving hearts; you are betrayers and murderers, and you maliciously killed the righteous Christ;
you received the law by the ordinance of angels, and you did not keep it." Then the Jews were greatly stirred in their hearts, and gnashed their teeth at him.
Then the holy Stephen was filled with the Holy Spirit, and looked toward heaven, and saw the glory of God, and the Saviour standing at his Father's right hand; and he said,
"Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand."
Then the Jews, crying out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and rushed upon him with one accord, and they seized him and led him out of the city to stone him.
Then the false witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man who was called Saul.
Then they began to pelt the blessed Stephen with hard stones; and he cried out and said, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."
And he bent his knees, calling out with a loud voice, "My Lord, do not lay these deeds against them as sin."
And with that word he departed to the Almighty Saviour, whom he had seen standing on high in heaven.
The wise Augustine spoke about this reading, and considered why the holy martyr Stephen said that he saw the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, and would not say the Son of God;

[?] since it seems to you more honourable to speak of Christ as the Son of God than as the Son of Man. But it was fitting that the Saviour should be revealed thus in heaven, and proclaimed thus on earth.
All the Jews' hostility arose from this: why should the Lord Christ, who according to the flesh is truly the Son of Man, also be called the Son of God?
Therefore the divine scripture very fittingly recorded that the Son of Man stood at God's right hand, to put to shame the unbelief of the Jews.
Christ was shown in heaven to his blessed martyr Stephen, who was killed on earth by unbelievers. Heavenly truth bore witness concerning him whom earthly wickedness had shamefully reviled.
Who can rightly be called the Son of Man except Christ alone, since every man is the child of two people, except him alone?
The blessed Stephen saw Christ standing because Christ was his helper in the spiritual battle of his martyrdom.
Truly, we confess in our creed that the Lord sits at his Father's right hand. A seat is fitting for a judge, and a standing place for helpers or fighters.
Now our faith confesses Christ's seat, because he is the true judge of the living and the dead. The blessed martyr Stephen saw him standing because he was his helper, as we said before.
The death of all chosen saints is precious in God's sight. Yet if any distinction can be made among martyrs, it seems that the highest is the one who established martyrdom after God.
Truly, Stephen was ordained a deacon at the hands of the apostles, but he went before them into the kingdom of heaven by a victorious death.
So he who was lower in rank became first in suffering, and he who was a disciple in order began to be a teacher in martyrdom.
Truly, the death that the Saviour deigned to suffer for mankind, Stephen was the first of men to give back to the Saviour.
He is called protomartyr, that is, the first martyr, because he was the first to suffer martyrdom after Christ's passion.
Stephen is a Greek name, which is in Latin Coronatus, which we say in English 'Crowned with glory'; because he has the eternal crown of glory, just as his name foretold of him.
The false witnesses who accused him were the first to begin stoning him,
because the law of Moses taught that whoever accused another to death had to throw the first stone at the one he had already killed with his tongue.
The fierce Jews stoned the saint in their rage, and he cried out and said, "Lord, do not hold these deeds against them as sin."
Now understand, my brothers, the great love of this blessed man. He was in the grip of death, and yet with true love he prayed for his killers.
and amid the falling of the stones, when anyone might have forgotten his dearest friends, he commended his enemies to God, saying thus,
"Lord, do not lay these deeds against them as sin." He grieved more for their sins than for his own wounds; more for their wickedness than for his own death;
and rightly more so, because eternal death followed their wickedness, and eternal life followed his death.
Saul held the clothes of the false witnesses and eagerly urged their minds on to the stoning. Stephen, on bended knees, prayed to the Lord to set Saul free.
Then God heard Stephen's prayer, and Saul was set free. The righteous man was heard, and the wicked man was justified.
In this deed it is shown how greatly the prayer of true love avails. Truly, God's church would not have had Paul as a teacher, if the holy martyr Stephen had not prayed so.
Behold, Paul now rejoices with Stephen in the kingdom of heaven. With Stephen he enjoys Christ's brightness, and with him he reigns.
Where Stephen went before, stoned to death with Saul's stones, Paul followed, helped by Stephen's prayers.
There Paul is not put to shame by Stephen's killing, but Stephen rejoices in Paul's fellowship, because true love rejoices in both of them.
True love overcame the cruelty of the Jews in Stephen, and the same love covered the great number of sins in Paul. In both of them together it earned the kingdom of heaven.
Therefore true love is the wellspring and origin of all good things, and a noble strength, and the way that leads to heaven.
Whoever walks in true love cannot go astray or be afraid: it guides, shields, and leads.
Through that true love this holy martyr was made so bold that he boldly rebuked the unbelief of the Jews, and he remained untroubled amid the great hailstones;
and he prayed benevolently for those stoning him, and moreover entered the heavenly hall alive and crowned with glory.
My brothers, let us imitate in some measure the faith of so great a teacher, and the love of so glorious a martyr.
Let us love our brothers in God's church with such a mind as this martyr then loved his enemies.
Be mindful of what the Truth himself promised in the holy gospel, and what pledge he gave us. The Saviour said,
"If you forgive the people who sin against you, then your Father will forgive you your sins; but if you will not forgive, your Father will not forgive you your offences either."
You hear now, my brothers, that through God's grace it lies in our own disposing how we will be judged by God. He said, "If you forgive, you will be forgiven."
Let no one deceive himself: truly, if anyone hates even one person in this world, whatever good he does, he loses it all; for the apostle Paul is not proved a liar, who said,
"Though I spend all my possessions on food for the poor, and though I give my own body to death, so that I burn in martyrdom;
if I do not have true love, it profits me nothing." Concerning the same, the evangelist John said,
"He who does not love his brother abides in death." Again he said, "Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer."
We who believe in God are all brothers, and we all say, "Pater noster qui es in celis," that is, "Our Father who art in heaven."
Let no one presume upon virginity without true love. Let no one trust in almsgiving or in prayers without the aforesaid love;
for as long as he holds that black hatred in his heart, he cannot by any means please the merciful God.
But if he wishes God to be merciful to him, then let him listen to good counsel, not from my mouth, but from Christ's own: he said,
"If you offer your gift at God's altar, and there you remember that your brother has something against you,
leave the gift at once before the altar, and go first to your brother and make peace with him; and then when you come back to the altar, offer your gift."
If, then, you have injured your Christian brother, he has something against you, and by God's teaching you must make amends to him before you offer your gift.
If, however, the Christian man who is your brother has done you harm in any way, you must forgive it mercifully.

Our spiritual gifts are our prayers, and hymns of praise, and the consecration of the Eucharist, and every other gift that we offer to God, which we must commit to God with a peaceable heart and brotherly love.
Now someone says against this reading, "I cannot love my enemy, whom I see every day being cruel toward me."
O man, you look at what your brother did to you, and you do not look at what you have done to God.
Since you have committed much heavier sins against God, why will you not forgive one person his little offences, so that Almighty God may forgive you the great sins?
Now you say again, "It is a great hardship for me to love my enemy and to pray for the one who seeks to do me harm."
We do not deny that it is a great labour; but if it is burdensome in this world, it comes to great reward in the world to come.
Truly, through love of your enemy you are God's friend; and not only are you his friend, but you are also God's child, through the condition that you love your enemy; just as Christ himself said,
"Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, so that you may be children of your Father, who is in heaven."
Anyone would readily endure many hardships and insults on condition that he might be counted as the child of some rich man, and as his heir to transitory possessions:

bear patiently now, for the sake of eternal honour, so that you may be counted children of God and his heirs in heavenly riches, what that other man would be willing to endure for a perishable livelihood.
We tell you God's law; keep it if you will. If we keep silent about it, we will not be saved.
The love of Christ compels us always to urge on the good, so that they may continue in goodness; and we admonish the wicked, so that they may quickly turn from their wickedness.
Let the righteous man not be careless in his beginning, nor the wicked man despair because of his unrighteousness. Let the good man fear that he may fall; let the wicked man strive to rise up.

Whoever is wicked, let him imitate Paul's conversion; whoever is good, let him persevere in goodness with Stephen; for no beginning is praiseworthy without a good ending. All praise is sung at the end.
My brothers, yesterday our Lord humbled himself to visit this world in true human nature:
now today the noble champion Stephen, departing from his bodily dwelling, went victorious to heaven.
Christ came down, clothed in flesh; Stephen went up, crowned with glory through his blood.
Yesterday the angels sang "Glory to God in the highest"; now today they received Stephen, rejoicing, into their fellowship, with whom he glories and rejoices forever in eternity. Amen.
